summary: Fixes limitations of the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) wildcard Forward Equivalence Class (FEC) by defining a Typed Wildcard FEC element and its procedures. It also adds an LDP capability for backward compatibility. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: A wildcard means everything, which is too broad. This lets a router say everything of one kind, like all the red balls, rather than every ball.

questions: what is a typed wildcard fec
difference between wildcard fec and typed wildcard fec
subtitle: A way for an LDP router to say 'all labels of this kind' in one message, with a capability to announce support.

tldr.problem: The Wildcard FEC element in LDP is untyped and works only in Label Withdraw and Label Release messages, so a router cannot name all FECs of one type or use a wildcard in a Label Request.
tldr.mechanism: A new Typed Wildcard FEC element (type 0x05) names the FEC element type to wildcard, and a new capability (0x050B) sent in Initialization messages tells peers it is supported.
tldr.outcome: A router can request, withdraw or release all label mappings of one FEC type in a single message. The RFC defines the typed wildcard for the Prefix FEC element only.

today: RFC 5918 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 7358.

sections.title: The Limits of the Untyped Wildcard
sections.content:
The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP, RFC 5036) hands out labels for Forwarding Equivalence Classes (FECs). Messages carry a FEC TLV that holds one or more FEC elements, each with a FEC type and an optional type-dependent value. RFC 5036 defines the Prefix and Wildcard types.

The Wildcard FEC element means all FECs, optionally limited to those bound to a given label. RFC 5918 names two deficiencies. It is untyped, so there is no way to say all FECs of a given type. And it may be used only in Label Withdraw and Label Release messages, not in Label Request messages.

The document defines a Typed Wildcard FEC element and its procedures, a capability announced at session setup, use in Label Request, and the typed wildcard for the Prefix FEC element. It does not change the procedures for the existing Wildcard FEC element.
sections.plainLanguage: The old 'everything' wildcard cannot be narrowed to one kind of thing, and cannot be used when asking for labels. This document fixes both.

sections.title: The Typed Wildcard FEC Element
sections.content:
The element refers to all FECs of a specified type that meet an optional constraint. It begins with a one-octet element type, 0x05, followed by a one-octet FEC Element Type naming the type to be wildcarded, and a one-octet Len FEC Type Info giving the length in octets of the optional type-specific information. That length MUST be 0 when there is no additional information.

If the additional information is absent, all FECs of the specified type match. Any future document that defines a new FEC element type should say whether typed wildcarding is needed for it, and if so, the length and format of the extra information.
sections.plainLanguage: The note says 'this is a typed wildcard', then which kind of thing it means, then how much extra detail follows, which may be none.

sections.title: Procedures
sections.content:
A Typed Wildcard FEC element MUST be the only FEC element in its TLV. If a receiver sees others, it should ignore them and process the message as if only the typed wildcard were present.

An implementation that supports the element MUST support it in Label Request, Label Withdraw and Label Release messages, and for every FEC element type defined in RFC 5036. A Label Request carrying it asks for one or more Label Mappings for all FECs of that type. In Label Withdraw or Label Release, if a Label TLV is present the element means all FECs of that type bound to that label; with no Label TLV it means all FECs of that type.

A router receiving a typed wildcard for a type it does not support, or one that does not support wildcarding, MUST stop decoding, abort the message and send an "Unknown FEC" Notification, as RFC 5036 already provides. It MAY also use mechanisms from RFC 5919, for example when it has no label bindings for the requested type.
sections.plainLanguage: The wildcard has to be the only item on the note, otherwise the extras are ignored. If a router does not understand the kind of thing named, it politely says so and stops.

sections.title: The Typed Wildcard FEC Capability
sections.content:
RFC 5036 already makes it safe to send an unsupported FEC element, but offers no way to learn whether a peer supports one except by trying. So an LDP speaker that supports the typed wildcard MUST announce it with a Typed Wildcard FEC Capability Parameter, defined with the mechanism of RFC 5561, in its Initialization messages only.

The capability TLV has type 0x050B and a length of 0x0001. The U and F bits MUST be 1 and 0, and the S bit MUST be 1 to show the capability is being advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: When two routers meet, each one says 'I know how to read typed wildcards', so nobody has to guess.

sections.title: The Prefix FEC Typed Wildcard
sections.content:
RFC 5036 defines the Prefix FEC element but no typed wildcard for it, so this RFC supplies one. The FEC Element Type is 0x02 (Prefix). Len FEC Type Info MUST be 0x0002, and the additional information is a two-octet Address Family taken from the IANA address family numbers registry. The procedures in section 4 apply.

No typed wildcard is needed for the Host FEC element from RFC 3036, which RFC 5036 removed, or for the Wildcard element, which is untyped by definition. The FEC Element Type field therefore MUST NOT be 0x01 or 0x03.
sections.plainLanguage: For the most common kind of thing, addresses, you say which family of addresses you mean, such as one kind of address book, and the router handles all of that kind.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned the code point 0x05 for the Typed Wildcard FEC element from the LDP FEC Type Name Space, and 0x050B for the Typed Wildcard FEC Capability from the TLV Type name space. Both come from the IETF Consensus range of the registries partitioned by RFC 5036.
sections.plainLanguage: Two official numbers were reserved so that nobody else uses them for something different.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: No security considerations apply beyond those of base LDP in RFC 5036, further described in RFC 5920. The RFC adds that the exposure could be seen as reduced: with a typed wildcard one message affects only the label mappings of one type, such as one address family, whereas the plain Wildcard FEC element can affect mappings of all types in one message.
sections.plainLanguage: Asking for only the red balls can do less accidental damage than asking for every ball.
